Phần A — Viết lại câu
1. Very few people can afford haute couture. — HAUTE COUTURE (n) = thời trang cao cấp, may đo riêng bởi các nhà mốt hàng đầu; từ mượn tiếng Pháp, giữ nguyên chính tả, không đọc âm "h" và "t" cuối.

2. Many clothing companies now operate on a fast-fashion model, churning out cheap trendy garments at breakneck speed. — FAST FASHION (n) = thời trang nhanh; khi đứng trước danh từ làm tính từ cần gạch nối ("fast-fashion model"), khi là danh từ độc lập thì không ("fast fashion is criticised").
3. He prefers a bespoke suit rather than something bought off the rack. — BESPOKE (adj) = may đo riêng theo yêu cầu; chủ yếu dùng trong tiếng Anh Anh, tiếng Anh Mỹ thường dùng "custom-made".

4. She loves buying vintage clothes and accessories instead of chasing whatever is currently popular. — VINTAGE (adj) = đồ cổ có giá trị từ một thời kỳ trước; phân biệt với "antique" (trên 100 năm tuổi) và "second-hand" (đồ cũ nói chung).

5. Rather than following short-lived fads, some shoppers prefer timeless pieces that never go out of style. — TIMELESS (adj) = vượt thời gian, kinh điển; mang nghĩa tích cực, khác với "outdated" (lỗi thời, tiêu cực).

6. Investigative reports have repeatedly shown that some garment factories operate as sweatshops, forcing employees to work long hours for very low pay. — SWEATSHOP (n) = xưởng bóc lột lao động; mang sắc thái phê phán mạnh, không dùng cho nhà máy có điều kiện tốt.

7. Trends on social media tend to be ephemeral, disappearing almost as quickly as they appear. — EPHEMERAL (adj) = chóng tàn, phù du; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai, tránh nhầm với "ethereal" (thanh tao).
8. A growing number of shoppers are trying to embrace sustainable fashion. — SUSTAINABLE FASHION (n phrase) = thời trang bền vững; là cụm cố định, không tách rời hai từ khi nói về phong trào này.

9. Wearing the same brand as everyone else can sometimes reflect conformity rather than genuine taste. — CONFORMITY (n) = sự rập khuôn, tuân theo chuẩn mực; đi với giới từ "to" ("conformity to trends"), không phải "with".

10. Designers are increasingly experimenting with a circular economy model, in which old garments are broken down and turned into new fabric. — CIRCULAR ECONOMY (n phrase) = kinh tế tuần hoàn; đối lập với "linear economy" (mô hình sản xuất-tiêu dùng-vứt bỏ).

11. Instead of throwing away an old pair of jeans, she upcycled it into a stylish new bag. — UPCYCLING (n, dùng động từ hoá "upcycle") = nâng cấp tái chế, biến vật liệu cũ thành sản phẩm có giá trị cao hơn; phân biệt với "recycling" (tái chế thành nguyên liệu thô, có thể giảm giá trị).
12. He always dresses to stand out from the crowd at every event he attends. — STAND OUT FROM THE CROWD (idiom) = nổi bật giữa đám đông; đi với giới từ "from", không phải "in" hay "of".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Fashion trends nowadays change extremely quickly, often disappearing within weeks. Band 8: Fashion trends are inherently ephemeral, cycling in and out of favour with bewildering speed.

2. Band 7: The fast-fashion industry produces a huge amount of waste that seriously harms the environment. Band 8: The fast-fashion industry generates staggering volumes of textile waste, exacting a heavy environmental toll.

3. Band 7: An increasing number of consumers are choosing to buy environmentally friendly clothing. Band 8: Sustainable fashion is gaining significant traction as consumers grow more environmentally conscious.

4. Band 7: Some people choose certain clothes mainly because they want to fit in with a particular group. Band 8: The pursuit of fashion is, for many, bound up with a deep-seated impulse towards social conformity.
5. Band 7: What people choose to wear can reveal a great deal about who they are. Band 8: Clothing functions as a potent medium through which individuals articulate their identity.

6. Band 7: Buying second-hand clothing has become an increasingly popular choice among younger generations. Band 8: Second-hand shopping has been thoroughly destigmatised among younger consumers, evolving from a mark of necessity into a badge of ethical style.

7. Band 7: It is often hard for ordinary consumers to find out exactly how the clothes they buy were produced. Band 8: Persistent opacity around sourcing and manufacturing leaves ordinary consumers largely unable to make informed, ethical purchasing decisions.

8. Band 7: Skilled craftsmanship is increasingly being pushed aside in favour of cheap, mass-produced clothing. Band 8: Traditional craftsmanship is being steadily eclipsed by low-cost mass production, a shift that arguably comes at the expense of quality and originality.

passages.text: In 2017, a 36-kilometre stretch of the Atacama desert in northern Chile became the unlikely destination for some 39,000 tonnes of unsold clothing. Most of the garments arrived in their original packaging, having traversed two or three continents before being deposited in a landscape so dry that synthetic fibres are expected to remain in the sand for several centuries. The Chilean import statistics that documented this trade were widely reported, briefly disturbing, and then largely absorbed. What the figures arguably exposed, in the view of the textile researcher Kate Fletcher at the University of the Arts London, was not the failure of the recycling system but the success of an upstream business model that had been operating, with very little friction, for more than two decades.

That business model, often summarised by the label "fast fashion", rests on three interlocking innovations: the compression of design-to-shelf cycles from months to weeks, the migration of garment manufacture to low-wage economies in South and South-East Asia, and the use of low-cost synthetics, particularly polyester, in place of cotton or wool. Industry analysts at McKinsey have estimated that global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2014, and that the average garment is now worn between seven and ten times before disposal, less than half the figure recorded in the early 1990s. The compounded effect, when annualised, exceeds the savings delivered by every per-garment efficiency programme reported across the same period. The structural consequence, according to the production economist Sandra Roos at the Swedish research institute RISE, is that the volume problem now overshadows the per-garment improvement that incremental efficiency gains can deliver.

The dominant policy response over the past decade has been the language of the circular economy: keep materials in use for longer, design out waste, and recover value at the end of life. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's influential 2017 report A New Textiles Economy projected that ambitious application of these principles could halve the apparel sector's carbon emissions by 2030. The vocabulary has been widely adopted, and not only by activists. Major brands now report on take-back schemes, recycled-content targets and durability metrics, and the European Union's 2022 Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles will, from 2025, require digital product passports for most garments sold in the bloc.

Whether these instruments will materially alter the picture remains contested. The Hong Kong-based industrial ecologist Christina Dean has argued that recycling technologies for blended fabrics, which make up the majority of contemporary garments, remain immature. Chemical recycling routes are improving rapidly, but their energy and solvent requirements complicate the carbon arithmetic, and mechanical recycling tends to degrade fibre quality with each cycle. Without a substantial increase in single-fibre garments and reliable separation infrastructure, the volume of textile waste that can be reincorporated into new clothing is, on present technology, limited to a single-digit percentage of the input stream.

A more fundamental critique focuses on volume itself. The geographer Lucy Norris has noted that virtually every prior wave of efficiency improvement in the global garment trade has been absorbed by additional consumption rather than translated into reduced material throughput. Cheaper clothes have, historically, been bought in greater numbers. If the circular-economy framework concentrates regulatory attention on what happens to garments after they leave the shop, while leaving the production volume itself largely unconstrained, Norris suggests that the result may be an industrial repair that does not, in aggregate, repair very much. Genuine progress, on this reading, will require interventions further upstream, including pricing mechanisms that internalise environmental costs and procurement rules that reward longevity over turnover.

Industry voices, predictably, contest the more pessimistic readings. A 2023 white paper from the Global Fashion Agenda, an industry-funded sustainability forum, argued that a combination of fibre-to-fibre recycling, design for disassembly and rental and resale platforms could plausibly reduce the sector's environmental footprint by thirty to forty per cent within a decade. The paper concedes, however, that this would require investment levels that no major brand has yet committed to publicly, and a degree of regulatory pressure that is unevenly distributed across producing countries. The optimism, in other words, is conditional rather than unconditional, and the conditions are not yet in place.

Some commentators have suggested that the term "sustainable fashion" itself has become a problem. The marketing scholar Aja Barber has argued that the label confers on consumers a sense of resolved obligation that the underlying data do not yet support; a garment branded as containing recycled fibres may still impose substantial upstream costs in water, energy and labour, and the rate of return-on-investment for repair and resale infrastructure remains, at the consumer scale, modest. The risk, in Barber's framing, is that a vocabulary intended to drive systemic change is instead being absorbed into the marketing apparatus of the very system it was meant to challenge. A reassuring label, on this account, can be the most effective form of resistance to the structural reforms that the same label superficially announces.

Where the literature appears to converge is on a hybrid recommendation. Targeted technical advances in recycling and design are likely to deliver real but partial gains. Without complementary regulation of production volume and pricing, however, those gains may be cancelled by the growth that the broader system continues to generate. The Atacama deposit, in that sense, is less a recycling failure than an indicator of the speed at which the upstream system produces. Whether the next decade of policy can address the upstream, rather than chiefly the downstream, may prove the most consequential question for the industry, and one whose answer remains, on the evidence currently available, unclear.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we're, um, hearing from Maya and Jonas on sustainable fashion supply-chain methodology. Maya, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname for me?
Yeah, sure. So I'm Maya Olusola — that's O-L-U-S-O-L-A, single word, no apostrophe. My dissertation tracked sixty-two micro-brands across the Lakeshore garment district. (Q1)

Erm, the pilot ran in 2020 — sorry, no, 2019 — and the main wave concluded in 2023. So four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2022, but the supply-chain freeze pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Tense-wise, just to clarify for the recording — your data collection FINISHED in 2023, and you're publishing this year, correct?
Right. Published 2026, but the next wave we're gonna run starts in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens here is what Professor Kebede called the "circular textile economy framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: closed-loop fashion, cradle-to-cradle apparel, regenerative clothing. All those describe the same construct. The current scholarly term, though, is circular textile economy. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Maya's framing. In my sample — thirty-one ateliers across the Copenhagen design quarter — most of the founders said they recycle pre-consumer offcuts INTO their next collection. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — twenty-three out of thirty-one, so roughly seventy-four per cent. Only a few — about thirteen per cent — discard offcuts entirely, and some — thirteen per cent also — incinerate them for biofuel. (Q4)
Right. Now, Maya, did your sample confirm the "consumers-drive-sustainability" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the micro-brands I observed did NOT regard consumer demand as the primary driver of their sustainability practices. The implicit market logic, well, has shifted. Today's micro-brand founders see it as a designer-led ethic, not a market-led response. Only a small minority — fewer than sixteen per cent — described demand as the dominant trigger. (Q5)

And, dunno about you, but I found something interesting on the rental-platform axis. So-called intensive rental — where platforms churn the same garment through dozens of wearers per season — that's actually rising sharply in higher-density urban markets. And the literature suggests this constrains a brand's capacity for premium positioning.
Hmm. Maya, did you control for price tier?
Kinda. We stratified by retail-price quartile. Counter-intuitively, the BOTTOM quartile reported the highest engagement with offcut reuse, not the top.
Well, it's about resource substitution — offcut reuse is cheaper than virgin fabric, so low-price brands lean on it harder.

And one final thing — collection-cycle data. In micro-brands with two collections per year, design fatigue was, um, considerably higher than in studios releasing four-plus collections. Researchers attribute it to scarcity of creative bandwidth.

Right. Now, going back to what Maya mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Jonas, on your seventy-four-per-cent figure: the implication that pre-consumer offcuts are de facto raw stock aligns with Kebede, but Maya's designer-ethic finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: The three pie charts compare the global fabric mix used to manufacture clothing in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, the period witnessed a pronounced shift away from natural materials toward synthetics, with polyester emerging as the dominant fibre. Meanwhile, a small but novel category of recycled blends appeared only in the most recent year.

In 1990, cotton was the staple of garment production, accounting for roughly half (49%) of all material used, followed by polyester at 21% and wool at 12%; natural fibres collectively represented around 71% of output. By 2010, this hierarchy had been inverted, as polyester rose sharply to 38%, overtaking cotton, which fell to 33%. Material proliferation also became evident, with other synthetic fibres climbing to 14%.

By 2024, polyester had reached a commanding 54%, while cotton more than halved compared with 1990 to just 22%. Other synthetic fibres edged up further to 16%, and wool dwindled to a marginal 3%. Significantly, recycled blends — a blended composition absent in earlier years — captured 5% of the market, hinting at modest sustainability progress.
The three pie charts illustrate how the global composition of materials used in clothing manufacture evolved across three benchmark years: 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, the most striking development was the wholesale displacement of natural fibres by synthetics, with polyester ascending to clear dominance. A novel category of recycled blends, meanwhile, surfaced only in the final year, gesturing towards a nascent sustainability agenda.

In 1990, cotton was the bedrock of garment production, commanding roughly half of all material at 49%, trailed by polyester at 21% and wool at 12%; natural fibres together constituted some 71% of output. Two decades later this hierarchy had been decisively overturned, as polyester surged to 38% and unseated cotton, which receded to 33%, while a broader array of other synthetics climbed to 14%.

It was by 2024, however, that the transformation reached its zenith. Polyester alone accounted for a commanding 54% — more than double its 1990 figure — whereas cotton had more than halved to a mere 22% and wool had dwindled to a negligible 3%. Most tellingly, recycled blends, entirely absent in earlier years, secured 5% of the market, signalling that environmental considerations were beginning, however tentatively, to reshape the industry.

blocks.text: The rise of fast fashion has, without question, transformed the way consumers buy and discard clothing. While the trend has democratised stylish dressing to a degree that would have been unthinkable a generation ago, I would argue that, on balance, its consequences are predominantly negative.

It is the speed and affordability of fast fashion that explain its dramatic success. Mass-produced garments now reach stores within weeks of appearing on the runway, allowing low-income consumers to wear trendy clothing for the first time. This democratising effect should not be dismissed lightly, particularly for young people for whom dressing the part can influence employment prospects. Some industry advocates also argue that cheap synthetic textiles reduce reliance on environmentally costly natural alternatives, though this claim is, in my view, considerably overstated.

The negative consequences, however, appear far more substantial. Environmentally, the production of polyester garments releases enormous quantities of microplastics into the oceans, and the industry is reportedly responsible for nearly ten percent of global carbon emissions. Socially, the breakneck production cycle relies heavily on unethical sweatshops in developing nations, where workers face dangerous conditions and minimal pay. Equally troubling is the rise of a disposable culture: items worn twice and discarded fuel landfill growth and undermine the slow-fashion ideal of timeless wardrobe staples.

In conclusion, while fast fashion has undeniably widened access to trendy clothing, the environmental and ethical costs tend to outweigh these gains. A shift toward ethical consumerism — favouring vintage pieces, durable garments and brands committed to sustainability — seems the more responsible path. Without such adjustments, the current model of buying and discarding clothing at breakneck speed is, in my opinion, simply unsustainable in the long run.

The advent of fast fashion has, arguably more than any other consumer trend of the past two decades, reshaped global dressing habits. While its democratising influence is real, I am persuaded that the environmental, ethical and cultural ramifications render this a largely negative development.

The consequences are best understood at three intersecting levels. Ecologically, the proliferation of synthetic textiles such as polyester releases hundreds of thousands of tons of microfibres into marine ecosystems annually, while the industry's carbon footprint rivals that of international aviation. So severe is the environmental toll that several European governments are now contemplating green taxes on disposable garments. At the social level, the breakneck production cycle is sustained by unethical sweatshops in low-wage economies, where the exploitation of textile workers remains chronically underreported. Culturally, meanwhile, a disposable mentality has supplanted the older logic of cherished wardrobe staples, eroding both craftsmanship and the bespoke traditions that once defined the industry.

Set against these harms are the genuine, if narrower, benefits. The democratisation of trendy clothing has allowed low-income consumers to look the part in professional settings, and the rapid turnover of styles satisfies the psychological appetite for novelty. Yet such gains, in my view, are increasingly difficult to defend when weighed against the long-term costs. Such is the velocity of contemporary consumption that the average garment is now worn only a handful of times before disposal — a pattern that no recycling scheme can fully offset.

In conclusion, while fast fashion has, to a limited extent, broadened access to fashionable attire, the preponderance of evidence suggests it is doing significant harm. A pivot toward ethical consumerism, including vintage purchases, the refurbishment of older garments and investment in timeless pieces, is, in my considered view, the only sustainable response to a model that has plainly outgrown its welcome.

Phần A — Viết lại câu
1. Very few people can afford haute couture. — HAUTE COUTURE (n) = thời trang cao cấp, may đo riêng bởi các nhà mốt hàng đầu; từ mượn tiếng Pháp, giữ nguyên chính tả, không đọc âm "h" và "t" cuối.

2. Many clothing companies now operate on a fast-fashion model, churning out cheap trendy garments at breakneck speed. — FAST FASHION (n) = thời trang nhanh; khi đứng trước danh từ làm tính từ cần gạch nối ("fast-fashion model"), khi là danh từ độc lập thì không ("fast fashion is criticised").
3. He prefers a bespoke suit rather than something bought off the rack. — BESPOKE (adj) = may đo riêng theo yêu cầu; chủ yếu dùng trong tiếng Anh Anh, tiếng Anh Mỹ thường dùng "custom-made".

4. She loves buying vintage clothes and accessories instead of chasing whatever is currently popular. — VINTAGE (adj) = đồ cổ có giá trị từ một thời kỳ trước; phân biệt với "antique" (trên 100 năm tuổi) và "second-hand" (đồ cũ nói chung).

5. Rather than following short-lived fads, some shoppers prefer timeless pieces that never go out of style. — TIMELESS (adj) = vượt thời gian, kinh điển; mang nghĩa tích cực, khác với "outdated" (lỗi thời, tiêu cực).

6. Investigative reports have repeatedly shown that some garment factories operate as sweatshops, forcing employees to work long hours for very low pay. — SWEATSHOP (n) = xưởng bóc lột lao động; mang sắc thái phê phán mạnh, không dùng cho nhà máy có điều kiện tốt.

7. Trends on social media tend to be ephemeral, disappearing almost as quickly as they appear. — EPHEMERAL (adj) = chóng tàn, phù du; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai, tránh nhầm với "ethereal" (thanh tao).
8. A growing number of shoppers are trying to embrace sustainable fashion. — SUSTAINABLE FASHION (n phrase) = thời trang bền vững; là cụm cố định, không tách rời hai từ khi nói về phong trào này.

9. Wearing the same brand as everyone else can sometimes reflect conformity rather than genuine taste. — CONFORMITY (n) = sự rập khuôn, tuân theo chuẩn mực; đi với giới từ "to" ("conformity to trends"), không phải "with".

10. Designers are increasingly experimenting with a circular economy model, in which old garments are broken down and turned into new fabric. — CIRCULAR ECONOMY (n phrase) = kinh tế tuần hoàn; đối lập với "linear economy" (mô hình sản xuất-tiêu dùng-vứt bỏ).

11. Instead of throwing away an old pair of jeans, she upcycled it into a stylish new bag. — UPCYCLING (n, dùng động từ hoá "upcycle") = nâng cấp tái chế, biến vật liệu cũ thành sản phẩm có giá trị cao hơn; phân biệt với "recycling" (tái chế thành nguyên liệu thô, có thể giảm giá trị).
12. He always dresses to stand out from the crowd at every event he attends. — STAND OUT FROM THE CROWD (idiom) = nổi bật giữa đám đông; đi với giới từ "from", không phải "in" hay "of".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Fashion trends nowadays change extremely quickly, often disappearing within weeks. Band 8: Fashion trends are inherently ephemeral, cycling in and out of favour with bewildering speed.

2. Band 7: The fast-fashion industry produces a huge amount of waste that seriously harms the environment. Band 8: The fast-fashion industry generates staggering volumes of textile waste, exacting a heavy environmental toll.

3. Band 7: An increasing number of consumers are choosing to buy environmentally friendly clothing. Band 8: Sustainable fashion is gaining significant traction as consumers grow more environmentally conscious.

4. Band 7: Some people choose certain clothes mainly because they want to fit in with a particular group. Band 8: The pursuit of fashion is, for many, bound up with a deep-seated impulse towards social conformity.
5. Band 7: What people choose to wear can reveal a great deal about who they are. Band 8: Clothing functions as a potent medium through which individuals articulate their identity.

6. Band 7: Buying second-hand clothing has become an increasingly popular choice among younger generations. Band 8: Second-hand shopping has been thoroughly destigmatised among younger consumers, evolving from a mark of necessity into a badge of ethical style.

7. Band 7: It is often hard for ordinary consumers to find out exactly how the clothes they buy were produced. Band 8: Persistent opacity around sourcing and manufacturing leaves ordinary consumers largely unable to make informed, ethical purchasing decisions.

8. Band 7: Skilled craftsmanship is increasingly being pushed aside in favour of cheap, mass-produced clothing. Band 8: Traditional craftsmanship is being steadily eclipsed by low-cost mass production, a shift that arguably comes at the expense of quality and originality.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
The Environmental Toll: The fashion industry is responsible for nearly 10% of global carbon emissions and is the second-largest consumer of the world's water supply.
Microplastic Pollution: Washing synthetic garments (like polyester and nylon) releases half a million tons of microfibers into the ocean annually.
The Rise of the Circular Economy: Thrift shopping, clothing rental platforms, and upcycling are becoming increasingly popular among Gen Z to combat the disposable culture.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Fast Fashion (Consumerism vs. Environment)

Reasons for Popularity: Democratises fashion, allowing low-income individuals to wear stylish, trendy clothing; rapid production cycles constantly satisfy the consumer's psychological desire for novelty.

Solutions to the Problem: Governments must impose strict "green taxes" on brands using synthetic textiles; consumers must adopt ethical consumerism by investing in durable wardrobe staples rather than disposable fads.
Topic: Designer Brands & Haute Couture (A waste of money?)
Why people buy them: Acts as a conspicuous status symbol to display wealth and social standing; bespoke items offer superior craftsmanship and longevity compared to mass-produced alternatives.
Why it's a waste: Consumers are often paying exorbitantly merely for a logo rather than actual material value; it fuels unhealthy societal materialism and peer pressure.
Topic: Dress Codes & Uniforms at Work/School

Arguments FOR Uniforms: Eliminates visual socioeconomic disparities among students/employees; fosters a strong sense of group identity and camaraderie; highly functional and saves time in the morning.

Arguments AGAINST Uniforms: Severely stifles individual self-expression; forces people to wear outmoded or uncomfortable garments; enforcing strict dress codes can lead to unnecessary micromanagement.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The fashion trend I'd like to discuss is the rise of the circular fashion economy — encompassing thrift shopping, clothing rental platforms, and upcycling — which has, in my view, fundamentally reshaped how a younger generation thinks about garments.

The movement gained serious traction around 2018-2019, propelled largely by Gen Z consumers reacting against the environmental devastation caused by fast fashion. To put the scale of the problem in context, the industry is responsible for nearly 10% of global carbon emissions and discharges half a million tonnes of microplastics into oceans annually — figures that are genuinely difficult to ignore.

The participants in this movement are remarkably diverse. On one end, you have platforms like Depop and Vinted — the latter valued at $5 billion — facilitating peer-to-peer second-hand trading at unprecedented scale. On another, rental services like Rent the Runway and HURR have made designer pieces accessible without the ownership burden. And then there are upcycling brands like Patagonia's Worn Wear, which actively repair and resell their own products rather than pushing endless novelty.

What I find particularly fascinating is the cultural reversal at play. Hand-me-downs and thrift store finds, which carried genuine social stigma in previous generations, have been thoroughly destigmatised — even valorised. Rarely has a consumer trend so cleanly aligned with environmental imperative.

Several factors explain my interest. Firstly, it represents a genuine paradigm shift away from disposable culture towards something resembling ethical consumerism. Secondly, the aesthetic itself — vintage layering, repurposed garments, deliberate imperfection — has produced some of the most creative individual styling we've seen in years. And thirdly, what really captivates me is the underlying philosophy: that style and sustainability needn't be mutually exclusive.

blocks.text: Q1: Should fashion brands disclose supply chains?

Point: Mandatory supply chain transparency for fashion brands is, in my view, both ethically necessary and increasingly inevitable — voluntary disclosure has manifestly failed to drive meaningful change.

Explain: The core problem is what economists call information asymmetry: consumers cannot make ethical choices when brands deliberately obscure where and how their garments are produced. Sweatshop conditions, child labour, and environmental violations thrive in this opacity, and self-regulation has proven woefully inadequate over three decades of trying.

Example: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse in Bangladesh, which killed 1,134 garment workers, exposed the brutal reality that even major brands like Primark and Walmart had no idea their products were being made in a building with visible structural cracks. Subsequently, the EU's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, adopted in 2024, now requires large fashion companies to map and disclose their entire supply chains — including subcontractors — with penalties up to 5% of global turnover. Brands like Everlane built their entire identity around "radical transparency", proving that disclosure is commercially viable.

Link: So while voluntary disclosure rarely happens at scale, regulatory frameworks combined with consumer pressure are slowly forcing supply chain visibility — and the brands that resist will likely find themselves on the wrong side of history.
Q2: Is sustainable fashion accessible?
Point: Sustainable fashion remains, frankly, considerably less accessible than its proponents like to claim — a fact that complicates the moral simplicity of "just buy ethical".

Explain: The fundamental issue is structural: sustainable production at small scale carries inherent cost premiums that fast fashion's economies of scale and labour exploitation deliberately undercut. A typical ethically-made T-shirt costs $35-50, compared to $5-10 from Shein, which puts genuine sustainability beyond the reach of households living paycheck to paycheck.

Example: A 2022 report by Wrap UK found that only 24% of British consumers regularly purchased sustainable clothing, with cost cited as the primary barrier by 58% of respondents. Conversely, second-hand and thrift markets — which are arguably the most sustainable option — have democratised access considerably; platforms like Vinted reported 65% year-on-year growth in 2022, particularly among lower-income demographics. Vietnam's burgeoning second-hand clothing markets, like Saigon Square, similarly offer sustainability through circularity rather than ethical premium pricing.

Link: This suggests that genuine accessibility lies less in convincing people to pay more for ethical labels and more in normalising circular consumption — buying less, buying second-hand, and extending garment lifespans through repair.
Q3: Has personal style died?

Point: I'd push back firmly on the notion that personal style has died — what we're actually witnessing is its democratisation and fragmentation, which can feel like death only if you confuse style with subcultural conformity.

Explain: The argument that personal style is dying typically points to algorithmically-driven micro-trends — coquette, balletcore, mob wife — that emerge and vanish within weeks, supposedly homogenising aesthetic choices. However, this conflates trend cycles with style itself; personal style has always existed alongside fashion trends, and arguably the explosion of subcultures online enables more individual expression, not less.

Example: Pre-internet fashion was actually far more uniform: in 1960s suburban America, you essentially had three or four dominant looks. Compare that to TikTok today, where simultaneously you find dark academia, gorpcore, Y2K revival, and a hundred other aesthetics flourishing in parallel. Social-media trend analyses have identified hundreds of distinct micro-aesthetics circulating in recent years, suggesting unprecedented stylistic pluralism rather than collapse.

Link: So rather than mourning the death of personal style, we should probably recognise that we're living through its most pluralistic era — the challenge is curation amid abundance, not scarcity of options.
T30 — FASHION & DESIGN
Lecture title: "Fast Fashion's Hidden Ledger, Sustainable Design and the Circular Wardrobe"
1. Section Type

IELTS Listening — Section 4 (academic lecture in sustainable design and fashion economics, ~3:00 minutes). Speaker: Dr Imani Adeyemi, Centre for Sustainable Textiles and Consumer Studies. Multiple-choice + matching hybrid.
2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

rows: rapid, low-cost production of trend-driven garments
a system designed to eliminate waste through reuse and recycling
design that minimises environmental and social harm
tiny synthetic strands shed by polyester garments during washing
to reuse material to make a product of higher value

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas
The lecturer will probably argue that fast fashion's low price disguises severe externalities.
Sustainable design will be reframed as a systemic, not merely material, challenge.
The circular economy may be defended as the only structurally viable response.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good morning. Today's lecture audits the true cost of the wardrobe — economically, environmentally and ethically. I will structure my argument around three claims: that fast fashion operates with a hidden ledger; that sustainable design must move beyond eco-labelling; and that only a fully circular economy can close the loop.

> Let me begin with the economics. The fast-fashion model — pioneered commercially by Zara and Inditex in the late 1990s — compressed the design-to-shelf cycle from roughly twelve months to as little as two weeks. The achievement is operationally remarkable and ecologically catastrophic. The industry now accounts for approximately ten percent of global carbon emissions and is the second-largest consumer of freshwater. The retail price you see at the till, in short, omits the wage subsidy borne by sweatshop labour and the ecological subsidy borne by the planet. Economists call these omissions externalities; I prefer the blunter term: unpaid invoices.

> Now, sustainable design. The first wave focused on eco-labelled materials — organic cotton, recycled polyester. Useful, but insufficient. The second wave, increasingly mainstream, attacks the design brief itself: garments engineered for durability, modular repair, disassembly at end of life, and reduced microfibre shedding. Stella McCartney and the Ellen MacArthur Foundation have been particularly influential here.

Now, while you find chart five, I want to puncture an optimism that often creeps into discussions of the circular economy — the comforting belief that recycling will quietly absolve the industry of its sins. It won't, and the chemistry explains why. Most garments today are blends — a poly-cotton T-shirt, say, or elastane woven through denim. [pause] Those fibre blends are, at present, fiendishly difficult to separate at end of life, which means the overwhelming majority of "recycled" textiles are in fact downcycled: turned into insulation, rags, mattress stuffing — a one-way descent in value, not the closed loop the brochures imply. Um, true fibre-to-fibre recycling, where a worn shirt becomes new shirt-grade yarn, remains a single-digit fraction of the waste stream.

Let me introduce a phenomenon the sustainability conversation has been slow to confront — the rebound effect, sometimes called Jevons' paradox. Here's the uncomfortable logic. When a garment is marketed as durable or organic or recycled, consumers frequently feel licensed to buy more of it, soothed by the green halo. So efficiency gains per item get swallowed by rising consumption volume. Well, a wardrobe of forty sustainably produced pieces can carry a larger footprint than ten conventional ones worn for a decade. The hard truth that eco-labelling obscures is that the most sustainable garment is, almost always, the one already hanging in your closet.

And there's a justice dimension I'd be remiss to omit. The waste we congratulate ourselves for "donating" doesn't vanish; much of it is baled and shipped to markets like Ghana's Kantamanto, where an estimated forty percent arrives unsellable and ends up clogging waterways and beaches. [pause] So the circular economy, if built carelessly, simply relocates the linear endpoint to someone else's coastline. Which forces the question of where responsibility ought legally to sit — with the consumer, the retailer, or the producer who designed the garment in the first place — and that question of accountability is precisely where I want to take us next…

> Finally, the circular economy. The orthodox linear model — take, make, dispose — must yield to a closed loop: take, make, use, repair, resell, recycle, remanufacture. Clothing rental platforms, thrift apps and upcycling workshops are the visible tip. Far more important is the infrastructure behind them: textile-sorting facilities, chemical recycling and producer-responsibility legislation. The wardrobe of the future, in short, will not be cheaper — but it ought to be honest. Now, please consult chart five…
5. Vocabulary Highlighted (band 8+ topic-specific)

fast fashion, design-to-shelf cycle, externalities, unpaid invoices, sweatshop labour, wage subsidy, eco-labelled materials, modular repair, disassembly, microfibre shedding, circular economy, closed loop, remanufacture, upcycling, producer-responsibility legislation, textile-sorting facilities, chemical recycling, ethical consumerism.
6. Five Questions (≥3 paraphrase)
Q1. (Note completion — paraphrase)
According to the lecturer, the fast-fashion model has shortened the design-to-shelf cycle from approximately twelve months down to as little as __________ weeks.
(Answer: two / 2)
Q2. (MCQ — paraphrase)

A. 1 percent
B. 5 percent
C. 10 percent
D. 25 percent
(Answer: C)
Q3. (Short answer — paraphrase)
What blunt two-word term does the lecturer prefer to use in place of externalities?
(Answer: unpaid invoices)
Q4. (MCQ — paraphrase / inference)
The lecturer argues that the second wave of sustainable design differs from the first because it…
A. focuses only on organic cotton
B. redesigns garments for durability, repair, disassembly and reduced microfibre shedding
C. rejects sustainability entirely
D. abandons recycled polyester
(Answer: B)
Q5. (Note completion — paraphrase)
In the circular model proposed by the lecturer, the linear sequence "take, make, dispose" must be replaced by a closed loop in which goods are repaired, resold, recycled and __________.
(Answer: remanufactured / remanufacture)
7. Listen-For Cues
Q1 cue: the contrastive interval "from roughly twelve months to as little as __________ weeks" — softener "as little as" precedes the figure.
Q2 cue: the institutional-style frame "The industry now accounts for approximately __________ of global carbon emissions" — percentage follows "approximately".
Q3 cue: the rebranding signal "Economists call these omissions externalities; I prefer the blunter term: __________" — answer follows the colon.
Q4 cue: the enumerated parallel "durability, modular repair, disassembly at end of life, and reduced microfibre shedding" — four-part list signals the inferential answer.
Q5 cue: the linear-to-circular reframing "take, make, use, repair, resell, recycle, __________" — the final verb in the chain is the answer.
8. Skills Box

rows: Catching contrastive time intervals ("from twelve months to…")

Tracking the final verb in a circular-economy chain

(a) Đề bài & biểu đồ / số liệu

Đề bài.  The three pie charts below show the proportion of materials used to manufacture clothing globally in 1990, 2010 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

•  Overview — a pronounced shift from natural to synthetic materials, polyester becoming dominant, with a new recycled category emerging; no figures.
•  Body 1 — describe 1990 (cotton-led, natural fibres dominant) and the 2010 reversal (polyester overtakes cotton).
•  Body 2 — describe 2024 (polyester commanding, cotton halved, recycled blends appear).
(d) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

Mô tả sự đảo ngôi năm 2010

Mô tả vị trí áp đảo năm 2024

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~176 từ)
The three pie charts compare the global fabric mix used to manufacture clothing in 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, the period witnessed a pronounced shift away from natural materials toward synthetics, with polyester emerging as the dominant fibre. Meanwhile, a small but novel category of recycled blends appeared only in the most recent year.

In 1990, cotton was the staple of garment production, accounting for roughly half (49%) of all material used, followed by polyester at 21% and wool at 12%; natural fibres collectively represented around 71% of output. By 2010, this hierarchy had been inverted, as polyester rose sharply to 38%, overtaking cotton, which fell to 33%. Material proliferation also became evident, with other synthetic fibres climbing to 14%.

By 2024, polyester had reached a commanding 54%, while cotton more than halved compared with 1990 to just 22%. Other synthetic fibres edged up further to 16%, and wool dwindled to a marginal 3%. Significantly, recycled blends — a blended composition absent in earlier years — captured 5% of the market, hinting at modest sustainability progress.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~198 từ)
The three pie charts illustrate how the global composition of materials used in clothing manufacture evolved across three benchmark years: 1990, 2010 and 2024.

Overall, the most striking development was the wholesale displacement of natural fibres by synthetics, with polyester ascending to clear dominance. A novel category of recycled blends, meanwhile, surfaced only in the final year, gesturing towards a nascent sustainability agenda.

In 1990, cotton was the bedrock of garment production, commanding roughly half of all material at 49%, trailed by polyester at 21% and wool at 12%; natural fibres together constituted some 71% of output. Two decades later this hierarchy had been decisively overturned, as polyester surged to 38% and unseated cotton, which receded to 33%, while a broader array of other synthetics climbed to 14%.

It was by 2024, however, that the transformation reached its zenith. Polyester alone accounted for a commanding 54% — more than double its 1990 figure — whereas cotton had more than halved to a mere 22% and wool had dwindled to a negligible 3%. Most tellingly, recycled blends, entirely absent in earlier years, secured 5% of the market, signalling that environmental considerations were beginning, however tentatively, to reshape the industry.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 mở Overview bằng tổng hợp sắc hơn ('the wholesale displacement of natural fibres by synthetics') và đặt hạng mục mới vào khung 'nascent sustainability agenda', trong khi Band 7 chỉ nêu xu hướng trực tiếp.

•  Band 8 dùng cleft ('It was by 2024 that the transformation reached its zenith') và lexis hiếm hơn ('the bedrock of', 'unseated', 'receded', 'dwindled to a negligible'), nâng Lexical Resource và Grammatical Range lên một bậc.

•  Band 8 kiểm soát so sánh bội số chính xác ('more than double its 1990 figure') và cohesion mượt với trạng từ đánh giá ('Most tellingly', 'however tentatively'), trong khi Band 7 mô tả tuần tự và đơn giản hơn.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Nhận diện cấu trúc 3 pie với hạng mục KHÔNG đồng nhất (30s): chú ý 'recycled blends' chỉ có ở 2024, 'other natural' biến mất ở 2024 — đọc kỹ nhãn từng pie.
•  Tìm 'mỏ neo' Overview (60s): xu hướng lớn nhất là sợi tự nhiên giảm — sợi tổng hợp tăng, polyester thống trị; hạng mục mới (recycled) xuất hiện. KHÔNG nêu số ở Overview.
•  Gom hạng mục theo nhóm (30s): natural (cotton + wool + other natural) vs synthetic (polyester + other synthetic) để mô tả khối thay vì 5 lát rời rạc.
•  Viết thân bài theo mốc năm: đoạn 2 gộp 1990 (cotton dẫn) + 2010 (đảo ngôi), đoạn 3 tập trung 2024 (polyester áp đảo + hạng mục mới).
•  Dùng so sánh bội số cho thay đổi mạnh ('more than halved', 'more than double'); chốt bằng nhận xét về hạng mục recycled mới nổi, TRÁNH bình luận ngoài dữ liệu.

Hệ quả tích cực (the benefits):

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~279 words)

The rise of fast fashion has, without question, transformed the way consumers buy and discard clothing. While the trend has democratised stylish dressing to a degree that would have been unthinkable a generation ago, I would argue that, on balance, its consequences are predominantly negative.

It is the speed and affordability of fast fashion that explain its dramatic success. Mass-produced garments now reach stores within weeks of appearing on the runway, allowing low-income consumers to wear trendy clothing for the first time. This democratising effect should not be dismissed lightly, particularly for young people for whom dressing the part can influence employment prospects. Some industry advocates also argue that cheap synthetic textiles reduce reliance on environmentally costly natural alternatives, though this claim is, in my view, considerably overstated.

The negative consequences, however, appear far more substantial. Environmentally, the production of polyester garments releases enormous quantities of microplastics into the oceans, and the industry is reportedly responsible for nearly ten percent of global carbon emissions. Socially, the breakneck production cycle relies heavily on unethical sweatshops in developing nations, where workers face dangerous conditions and minimal pay. Equally troubling is the rise of a disposable culture: items worn twice and discarded fuel landfill growth and undermine the slow-fashion ideal of timeless wardrobe staples.

In conclusion, while fast fashion has undeniably widened access to trendy clothing, the environmental and ethical costs tend to outweigh these gains. A shift toward ethical consumerism — favouring vintage pieces, durable garments and brands committed to sustainability — seems the more responsible path. Without such adjustments, the current model of buying and discarding clothing at breakneck speed is, in my opinion, simply unsustainable in the long run.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~300 words)

The advent of fast fashion has, arguably more than any other consumer trend of the past two decades, reshaped global dressing habits. While its democratising influence is real, I am persuaded that the environmental, ethical and cultural ramifications render this a largely negative development.

The consequences are best understood at three intersecting levels. Ecologically, the proliferation of synthetic textiles such as polyester releases hundreds of thousands of tons of microfibres into marine ecosystems annually, while the industry's carbon footprint rivals that of international aviation. So severe is the environmental toll that several European governments are now contemplating green taxes on disposable garments. At the social level, the breakneck production cycle is sustained by unethical sweatshops in low-wage economies, where the exploitation of textile workers remains chronically underreported. Culturally, meanwhile, a disposable mentality has supplanted the older logic of cherished wardrobe staples, eroding both craftsmanship and the bespoke traditions that once defined the industry.

Set against these harms are the genuine, if narrower, benefits. The democratisation of trendy clothing has allowed low-income consumers to look the part in professional settings, and the rapid turnover of styles satisfies the psychological appetite for novelty. Yet such gains, in my view, are increasingly difficult to defend when weighed against the long-term costs. Such is the velocity of contemporary consumption that the average garment is now worn only a handful of times before disposal — a pattern that no recycling scheme can fully offset.

In conclusion, while fast fashion has, to a limited extent, broadened access to fashionable attire, the preponderance of evidence suggests it is doing significant harm. A pivot toward ethical consumerism, including vintage purchases, the refurbishment of older garments and investment in timeless pieces, is, in my considered view, the only sustainable response to a model that has plainly outgrown its welcome.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (đảo ngữ 'So severe is the environmental toll that...', 'Such is the velocity of contemporary consumption that...', đảo ngữ 'Set against these harms are...') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft mở bài.

•  Band 8 huy động nominalisation dày đặc ('the proliferation of synthetic textiles', 'the exploitation of textile workers', 'the democratisation of trendy clothing') và lexis Band 8 ('cultural ramifications', 'bespoke traditions'), nâng Lexical Resource một bậc.

•  Band 8 tổ chức hệ quả theo ba tầng tường minh (ecological / social / cultural) với register học thuật nhất quán, trong khi Band 7 vẫn còn cụm hơi đời thường ('should not be dismissed lightly', 'simply unsustainable in the long run').

vocabulary.common_error: Từ mượn tiếng Pháp, giữ nguyên chính tả; phát âm 'haute' gần như 'oat', không đọc âm 'h' và 't' cuối.
vocabulary.definition_en: the creation of exclusive, custom-fitted clothing by leading fashion houses, made with the finest materials
vocabulary.definition_vi: thời trang cao cấp
vocabulary.example: Few people can afford haute couture, but its designs often influence trends that trickle down to high-street fashion.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tiếng Pháp 'haute' (cao) + 'couture' (may vá) → may đo ở đẳng cấp cao nhất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thời trang nhanh — mô hình sản xuất hàng loạt quần áo giá rẻ, bắt kịp xu hướng nhanh chóng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> For years, the dominant model has been **fast fashion** — a system where trendy garments are churned out at breakneck speed.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'fast' (nhanh) + 'fashion' (thời trang) → sản xuất và tiêu thụ quần áo với tốc độ chóng mặt.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng như tính từ trước danh từ, thêm gạch nối: 'fast-fashion brands', nhưng khi là danh từ độc lập thì không cần: 'fast fashion is criticised'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the mass production of inexpensive clothing rapidly in response to the latest trends
vocabulary.definition_vi: thời trang nhanh
vocabulary.example: For years, the dominant model has been fast fashion — a system where trendy garments are churned out at breakneck speed.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'fast' (nhanh) + 'fashion' (thời trang) → sản xuất và tiêu thụ quần áo với tốc độ chóng mặt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
May đo riêng — được thiết kế, tạo ra riêng cho một khách hàng cụ thể theo yêu cầu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He prefers a **bespoke** suit tailored precisely to his measurements rather than something bought off the rack.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Xuất phát từ 'be spoken for' (đã được đặt trước) → vải đã được 'nói trước' là dành riêng cho một khách hàng.
vocabulary.common_error: Chủ yếu dùng ở Anh-Anh; Anh-Mỹ thường dùng 'custom-made' hoặc 'made-to-order' thay thế.
vocabulary.definition_en: made for a particular customer or user; custom-made to specific requirements
vocabulary.definition_vi: may đo riêng, thiết kế theo yêu cầu
vocabulary.example: He prefers a bespoke suit tailored precisely to his measurements rather than something bought off the rack.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Xuất phát từ 'be spoken for' (đã được đặt trước) → vải đã được 'nói trước' là dành riêng cho một khách hàng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đồ vintage — trang phục hoặc vật phẩm chất lượng cao từ một thời kỳ trước, được đánh giá cao vì tuổi đời và phong cách.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This movement also promotes buying **vintage** clothing rather than chasing fleeting fads.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc từ rượu vang 'vintage wine' (rượu theo năm sản xuất) → mở rộng sang thời trang 'đồ xưa chất lượng'.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'vintage' (đồ cũ có giá trị, đặc trưng cho một thời kỳ) với 'antique' (đồ cổ, thường trên 100 năm tuổi) hay 'second-hand' (đồ cũ nói chung, không nhất thiết có giá trị).
vocabulary.definition_en: denoting or relating to high-quality clothing or items from an earlier period, valued for their age and style
vocabulary.definition_vi: đồ cổ, đồ xưa (có giá trị)
vocabulary.example: This movement also promotes buying vintage clothing rather than chasing fleeting fads.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc từ rượu vang 'vintage wine' (rượu theo năm sản xuất) → mở rộng sang thời trang 'đồ xưa chất lượng'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vượt thời gian — không bị ảnh hưởng bởi sự thay đổi của thời gian hay xu hướng; kinh điển và bền vững.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It advocates for sustainable practices, encouraging consumers to seek out high-quality pieces that are **timeless**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'time' (thời gian) + '-less' (không có) → không bị ảnh hưởng bởi thời gian → vượt thời gian.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Timeless' mang nghĩa tích cực (kinh điển, không lỗi mốt), khác với 'outdated' (lỗi thời, nghĩa tiêu cực).
vocabulary.definition_en: not affected by the passage of time or changes in fashion; classic and enduring in style
vocabulary.definition_vi: vượt thời gian, kinh điển
vocabulary.example: It advocates for sustainable practices, encouraging consumers to seek out high-quality pieces that are timeless.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'time' (thời gian) + '-less' (không có) → không bị ảnh hưởng bởi thời gian → vượt thời gian.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Xưởng bóc lột lao động — nơi công nhân làm việc nhiều giờ với lương thấp trong điều kiện tồi tệ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> To keep prices artificially low, some brands rely heavily on unethical **sweatshops** in developing countries.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sweat' (mồ hôi) + 'shop' (xưởng) → nơi công nhân phải đổ mồ hôi làm việc trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ mang tính phê phán mạnh; không dùng để mô tả một nhà máy bình thường có điều kiện lao động tốt.
vocabulary.definition_en: a factory or workshop, especially in the clothing industry, where workers are employed for long hours at low wages in poor conditions
vocabulary.definition_vi: xưởng bóc lột lao động
vocabulary.example: To keep prices artificially low, some brands rely heavily on unethical sweatshops in developing countries.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sweat' (mồ hôi) + 'shop' (xưởng) → nơi công nhân phải đổ mồ hôi làm việc trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tổng hợp, nhân tạo — được tạo ra bằng phương pháp tổng hợp hoá học để bắt chước sản phẩm tự nhiên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The production of **synthetic** textiles like polyester releases harmful microplastics into the oceans.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'synthesis' (tổng hợp) + -ic → synthetic → được tạo ra qua quá trình tổng hợp hoá học.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'synthetic' (nhân tạo, do hoá học tạo ra) với 'artificial' (nhân tạo nói chung, phạm vi rộng hơn, không nhất thiết qua tổng hợp hoá học).
vocabulary.definition_en: made by chemical synthesis, especially to imitate a natural product; man-made
vocabulary.definition_vi: tổng hợp, nhân tạo
vocabulary.example: The production of synthetic textiles like polyester releases harmful microplastics into the oceans.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'synthesis' (tổng hợp) + -ic → synthetic → được tạo ra qua quá trình tổng hợp hoá học.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thẩm mỹ — liên quan đến vẻ đẹp hoặc sự thưởng thức cái đẹp; đẹp mắt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Her unique **aesthetic** sense allows her to combine unconventional colours in a way that always looks harmonious.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp 'aisthesis' (cảm nhận) → aesthetic → liên quan đến việc cảm nhận và đánh giá cái đẹp.
vocabulary.common_error: Có thể dùng như tính từ ('an aesthetic quality') hoặc danh từ không đếm được ('a designer's aesthetic' = phong cách thẩm mỹ riêng).
vocabulary.definition_en: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty; visually pleasing
vocabulary.definition_vi: thẩm mỹ, mang tính thẩm mỹ
vocabulary.example: Her unique aesthetic sense allows her to combine unconventional colours in a way that always looks harmonious.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'aisthesis' (cảm nhận) → aesthetic → liên quan đến việc cảm nhận và đánh giá cái đẹp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chóng tàn — chỉ tồn tại trong một khoảng thời gian rất ngắn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Ephemeral** fashion trends dominate social media, disappearing from relevance almost as quickly as they arrive.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp 'ephemeros' (kéo dài một ngày) → ephemeral → chỉ tồn tại trong thời gian rất ngắn.
vocabulary.common_error: Trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai; đừng nhầm với 'ethereal' (thanh tao, mong manh) — hai từ khác nghĩa dù âm gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: lasting for only a very short time; short-lived
vocabulary.definition_vi: chóng tàn, phù du
vocabulary.example: Ephemeral fashion trends dominate social media, disappearing from relevance almost as quickly as they arrive.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'ephemeros' (kéo dài một ngày) → ephemeral → chỉ tồn tại trong thời gian rất ngắn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thời trang bền vững — sản xuất và tiêu dùng quần áo theo cách giảm thiểu tác hại đến môi trường và xã hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> More consumers are choosing to embrace **sustainable fashion** by buying fewer, higher-quality garments.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sustain' (duy trì lâu dài) + 'fashion' → thời trang được sản xuất và tiêu dùng theo cách có thể duy trì lâu dài, không gây hại môi trường.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi liền với danh từ như một cụm cố định; đừng tách rời 'sustainable' và 'fashion' khi dùng như một khái niệm phong trào.
vocabulary.definition_en: clothing produced and consumed in ways that minimise environmental and social harm
vocabulary.definition_vi: thời trang bền vững
vocabulary.example: More consumers are choosing to embrace sustainable fashion by buying fewer, higher-quality garments.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sustain' (duy trì lâu dài) + 'fashion' → thời trang được sản xuất và tiêu dùng theo cách có thể duy trì lâu dài, không gây hại môi trường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự rập khuôn — hành vi tuân theo các chuẩn mực xã hội được chấp nhận, thường qua bắt chước người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Wearing the same designer labels as everyone else can reflect a deeper social **conformity** rather than genuine personal taste.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'conform' (tuân theo) + -ity → conformity → xu hướng làm giống người khác, tuân theo số đông.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'to': 'conformity to social norms', không phải 'conformity with' trong hầu hết ngữ cảnh học thuật.
vocabulary.definition_en: behaviour that matches accepted social standards or norms, often through imitation of others
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự rập khuôn, tuân theo chuẩn mực
vocabulary.example: Wearing the same designer labels as everyone else can reflect a deeper social conformity rather than genuine personal taste.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'conform' (tuân theo) + -ity → conformity → xu hướng làm giống người khác, tuân theo số đông.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính biểu tượng — được công nhận rộng rãi và đại diện cho những giá trị hoặc ý tưởng nhất định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Chanel's little black dress remains one of the most **iconic** designs in fashion history.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'icon' (biểu tượng) + -ic → iconic → mang tính biểu tượng, được công nhận rộng rãi.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng lạm dụng 'iconic' cho mọi thứ nổi tiếng; đúng nghĩa nó chỉ những gì mang tính biểu tượng, đại diện lâu dài cho một giá trị hay phong cách.
vocabulary.definition_en: widely recognised and considered to represent particular values or ideas; symbolically famous
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính biểu tượng
vocabulary.example: Chanel's little black dress remains one of the most iconic designs in fashion history.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'icon' (biểu tượng) + -ic → iconic → mang tính biểu tượng, được công nhận rộng rãi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kinh tế tuần hoàn — mô hình kinh tế hướng đến loại bỏ lãng phí bằng cách tái sử dụng, sửa chữa và tái chế liên tục.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Fashion brands are increasingly investing in a **circular economy** model, where old garments are recycled into new fabric.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'circular' (hình tròn, khép kín) + 'economy' → tài nguyên đi theo vòng tròn khép kín, không bị lãng phí.
vocabulary.common_error: Khái niệm kinh tế học chuyên ngành, đối lập với 'linear economy' (mô hình sản xuất-tiêu dùng-vứt bỏ truyền thống).
vocabulary.definition_en: an economic model designed to eliminate waste through the continual reuse, repair, and recycling of resources
vocabulary.definition_vi: kinh tế tuần hoàn
vocabulary.example: Fashion brands are increasingly investing in a circular economy model, where old garments are recycled into new fabric.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'circular' (hình tròn, khép kín) + 'economy' → tài nguyên đi theo vòng tròn khép kín, không bị lãng phí.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nâng cấp tái chế — biến vật liệu hoặc sản phẩm bị bỏ đi thành món đồ mới có chất lượng hoặc giá trị cao hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some independent designers specialise in **upcycling** old denim into entirely new, one-of-a-kind jackets.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'up' (nâng lên) + 'cycling' (chu trình, tái sử dụng) → biến đồ cũ thành thứ có giá trị cao hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'upcycling' (nâng chất lượng vật liệu cũ thành sản phẩm mới có giá trị cao hơn) với 'recycling' (tái chế thành nguyên liệu thô, có thể giảm giá trị).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of transforming discarded materials or products into new items of higher quality or value
vocabulary.definition_vi: nâng cấp tái chế, biến rác thành đồ có giá trị cao hơn
vocabulary.example: Some independent designers specialise in upcycling old denim into entirely new, one-of-a-kind jackets.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'up' (nâng lên) + 'cycling' (chu trình, tái sử dụng) → biến đồ cũ thành thứ có giá trị cao hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng có đạo đức — thói quen mua sắm dựa trên cân nhắc về tác động đạo đức, xã hội và môi trường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Ethical consumerism** has encouraged shoppers to research a brand's labour practices before making a purchase.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'ethical' (có đạo đức) + 'consumerism' (chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng) → mua sắm có cân nhắc đến đạo đức, môi trường.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được; đừng nhầm với 'consumerism' đơn thuần (chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng, thường mang nghĩa tiêu cực về mua sắm quá mức).
vocabulary.definition_en: the practice of purchasing products based on their ethical, social, and environmental impact
vocabulary.definition_vi: chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng có đạo đức
vocabulary.example: Ethical consumerism has encouraged shoppers to research a brand's labour practices before making a purchase.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ethical' (có đạo đức) + 'consumerism' (chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng) → mua sắm có cân nhắc đến đạo đức, môi trường.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng vi sợi bong ra — các sợi vải tổng hợp siêu nhỏ thoát ra từ quần áo khi giặt, gây ô nhiễm nguồn nước.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Microfibre shedding** from synthetic clothing during washing machine cycles is now recognised as a major source of ocean microplastic pollution.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'micro-' (siêu nhỏ) + 'fibre' (sợi) + 'shedding' (rụng, bong ra) → những sợi vải siêu nhỏ bong ra khi giặt, gây ô nhiễm.
vocabulary.common_error: Thuật ngữ khoa học môi trường chuyên sâu; không nhầm với 'shedding' thông thường (rụng lông, tóc) — ở đây chỉ sợi vải tổng hợp.
vocabulary.definition_en: the release of tiny synthetic fibres from clothing, especially during washing, which pollute waterways
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiện tượng vi sợi tổng hợp bong ra (gây ô nhiễm nước)
vocabulary.example: Microfibre shedding from synthetic clothing during washing machine cycles is now recognised as a major source of ocean microplastic pollution.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'micro-' (siêu nhỏ) + 'fibre' (sợi) + 'shedding' (rụng, bong ra) → những sợi vải siêu nhỏ bong ra khi giặt, gây ô nhiễm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ăn mặc cực kỳ lộng lẫy, gây ấn tượng mạnh với người xung quanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She arrived at the prestigious gala **dressed to kill** in a stunning red gown.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'kill' ở đây hiểu theo nghĩa bóng 'gây choáng ngợp' → ăn mặc đẹp đến mức khiến người khác 'ngã gục'.
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom mang nghĩa tích cực (ăn mặc đẹp gây ấn tượng), không liên quan gì đến bạo lực dù có từ 'kill'.
vocabulary.definition_en: wearing extremely attractive or stylish clothes, intended to impress or attract attention
vocabulary.definition_vi: ăn mặc cực kỳ lộng lẫy, gây ấn tượng mạnh
vocabulary.example: She arrived at the prestigious gala dressed to kill in a stunning red gown.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'kill' ở đây hiểu theo nghĩa bóng 'gây choáng ngợp' → ăn mặc đẹp đến mức khiến người khác 'ngã gục'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vừa như in — trang phục vừa vặn hoàn hảo với cơ thể, như được may đo riêng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I bought this tailored suit without trying it on, but it **fits like a glove**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một chiếc găng tay ôm khít từng ngón tay → quần áo vừa vặn hoàn hảo trên cơ thể.
collocations: the dress fits her like a glove
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định, không thay đổi 'glove' thành số nhiều hay vật dụng khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: to fit a person's body perfectly, as if custom-made
vocabulary.definition_vi: vừa như in, khít hoàn hảo
vocabulary.example: I bought this tailored suit without trying it on, but it fits like a glove.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một chiếc găng tay ôm khít từng ngón tay → quần áo vừa vặn hoàn hảo trên cơ thể.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
May sẵn — quần áo được sản xuất theo kích cỡ tiêu chuẩn, không phải may đo riêng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He buys expensive business suits **off the rack** because he hates waiting for tailors.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'off the rack' (lấy thẳng từ giá treo đồ) → quần áo may sẵn, không cần đặt riêng.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng như tính từ trước danh từ, cần gạch nối: 'an off-the-rack suit'; khi là trạng ngữ sau động từ thì không cần: 'buy it off the rack'.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of clothing) ready-made and sold in standard sizes, rather than custom-tailored
vocabulary.definition_vi: may sẵn (không phải đo riêng)
vocabulary.example: He buys expensive business suits off the rack because he hates waiting for tailors.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'off the rack' (lấy thẳng từ giá treo đồ) → quần áo may sẵn, không cần đặt riêng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đồ mặc lại — quần áo được truyền lại từ người khác, thường là từ anh/chị sang em.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> As the youngest child, I always had to wear my older brother's **hand-me-downs**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'hand' (trao tay) + 'me' + 'down' (xuống, cho người nhỏ tuổi hơn) → đồ được trao lại cho người sau.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ ghép có gạch nối; thường dùng ở số nhiều 'hand-me-downs' khi nói chung về quần áo cũ được truyền lại.
vocabulary.definition_en: a piece of clothing that has been passed down from one person, often an older sibling, to a younger one
vocabulary.definition_vi: đồ mặc lại (từ anh chị truyền xuống)
vocabulary.example: As the youngest child, I always had to wear my older brother's hand-me-downs.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'hand' (trao tay) + 'me' + 'down' (xuống, cho người nhỏ tuổi hơn) → đồ được trao lại cho người sau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nạn nhân của thời trang — người chạy theo xu hướng một cách mù quáng, mặc đồ không hợp với bản thân.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Don't be a **fashion victim**; you should only wear what actually suits your body shape.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'fashion' (thời trang) + 'victim' (nạn nhân) → người bị thời trang 'bắt làm nạn nhân' vì chạy theo mù quáng.
vocabulary.common_error: Mang sắc thái châm biếm nhẹ; không nhầm với 'fashionista' (người có gu thời trang tốt, sắc thái tích cực hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who follows current trends too closely, often wearing clothes that do not suit them
vocabulary.definition_vi: nạn nhân của thời trang (chạy theo mốt một cách mù quáng)
vocabulary.example: Don't be a fashion victim; you should only wear what actually suits your body shape.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'fashion' (thời trang) + 'victim' (nạn nhân) → người bị thời trang 'bắt làm nạn nhân' vì chạy theo mù quáng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trông đúng chuẩn — có vẻ ngoài phù hợp với một vai trò, công việc hoặc địa vị cụ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> If you want to be promoted to manager, you need to dress up and **look the part**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'look' (trông như) + 'the part' (vai diễn) → ăn mặc đúng như đang đóng đúng vai trò của mình.
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định với mạo từ 'the'; không nói 'look a part' hay 'look parts'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to have an appearance that matches a particular role, job, or status
vocabulary.definition_vi: trông đúng chuẩn (với vai trò, vị trí của mình)
vocabulary.example: If you want to be promoted to manager, you need to dress up and look the part.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'look' (trông như) + 'the part' (vai diễn) → ăn mặc đúng như đang đóng đúng vai trò của mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nổi bật giữa đám đông — khác biệt rõ rệt hoặc vượt trội so với những người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Her unique and bold style allows her to effortlessly **stand out from the crowd**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'stand out' (nổi lên) + 'from the crowd' (khỏi đám đông) → khác biệt, dễ nhận ra giữa số đông.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'from', không phải 'in' hay 'of': 'stand out from the crowd'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be noticeably different from, or better than, everyone else in a group
vocabulary.definition_vi: nổi bật giữa đám đông
vocabulary.example: Her unique and bold style allows her to effortlessly stand out from the crowd.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'stand out' (nổi lên) + 'from the crowd' (khỏi đám đông) → khác biệt, dễ nhận ra giữa số đông.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tốn kém quá mức — tiêu tốn nhiều tiền hơn khả năng chi trả, cháy túi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Buying designer brands can easily **break the bank** if you are not careful with your budget.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh 'phá vỡ ngân hàng' → tiêu tốn hết sạch tiền tiết kiệm.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng ở dạng phủ định 'won't break the bank' để nhấn mạnh giá cả phải chăng.
vocabulary.definition_en: to cost far more money than one can afford; to use up all of one's money
vocabulary.definition_vi: tốn kém quá mức, cháy túi
vocabulary.example: Buying designer brands can easily break the bank if you are not careful with your budget.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình ảnh 'phá vỡ ngân hàng' → tiêu tốn hết sạch tiền tiết kiệm.
